query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal oxidation treatment that induces the in-situ formation of an ultrathin, adherent spinel oxide layer on the HEA surface will simultaneously reduce the coefficient of friction and wear rate by approximately 20–30% and 50%, respectively, over a wide service-temperature range (from room temperature to ~500°C).
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated high-entropy alloy (HEA) used in self‐lubricating moving components, which exhibits high friction and wear across a wide temperature range.
generation.intervention: A single-step controlled thermal oxidation process performed under a tailored atmosphere (with a calibrated oxygen partial pressure) to promote the in-situ formation of a spinel oxide layer.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied such that the spinel oxide film forms reproducibly on the HEA surface and remains stable from ambient temperature up to approximately 500°C during operation.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrathin, adherent spinel oxide layer formed on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The spinel oxide layer acts as a protective, lubricious barrier that minimizes direct asperity contact between moving surfaces. This barrier reduces friction and wear by lowering shear stresses and distributing load, thereby mitigating mechanical degradation during high-temperature operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the treated alloy is expected to show a roughly 20–30% reduction in the coefficient of friction and about a 50% lower wear rate across the full service temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA forms non-optimized oxide layers (or none at all) leading to higher friction and wear under variable operational temperatures.
generation.boundary: The approach may not be effective if the oxidation process conditions deviate significantly (e.g., improper oxygen partial pressure or heating rate) from those required for forming the optimal ultrathin spinel film, or if the operational temperature falls outside the designated range.
generation.uncertainty: Precise process parameters to achieve the ideal film thickness and adherence are not fully established, and the degree of friction and wear improvement may vary depending on minor variations in processing and operational conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set undergoing the tailored thermal oxidation treatment and one untreated control. Subject both sets to reciprocating wear tests across a range of temperatures from ambient to 500°C within a controlled atmosphere. Characterize the oxide film using microscopy and surface analysis to confirm its formation and uniformity.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at various temperatures
Wear rate (mass loss or depth of wear track) under standardized load conditions
Surface oxide layer thickness and composition via SEM/TEM and XPS analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (at least 20–30% lower friction and 50% lower wear rate) compared to untreated samples across the prescribed temperature range, or if the intended spinel oxide layer is not reliably formed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloys for moving components focused on understanding mechanical deformation and wear behavior under various conditions. In particular, research on the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA (PMC7515071) showed that under elevated temperatures, the alloy’s wear rate dropped significantly when a spinel phase formed in the wear track. Further work on refractory and nanocrystalline HEA films (e.g., PMC7304825) has emphasized tribological performance improvements through processing routes but has struggled to achieve a single, robust intervention that simultaneously lowers friction and wear across ambient and high temperature conditions.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence that in-situ surface oxide films (such as spinels) can enhance high-temperature wear resistance, no single-step surface engineering approach has been demonstrated to reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate uniformly over a wide service-temperature range, particularly without resorting to multi-step treatments or composite fabrications.
decision.lever: Controlled in-situ formation of an ultrathin, adherent spinel oxide layer via a tailored oxidation process (e.g., optimized thermal oxidation under controlled atmosphere conditions)
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the observed benefits of high-temperature spinel formation seen in PMC7515071. By engineering the surface to reproducibly form a lubricious spinel film over the entire operational temperature range, the intervention capitalizes on a proven low-friction, wear-minimizing mechanism in a single, streamlined step. This lever targets the critical interface where friction and wear originate and is anticipated to yield a 20–30% reduction in friction and a 50% lower wear rate compared to untreated HEA, with experimental falsification achievable through high-temperature reciprocating wear tests that measure deviations from the expected friction and wear performance.
